newsitem.title: ARMENIA: Ter-Petrosyan declared winner, troops stay put.
newsitem.headline: Ter-Petrosyan declared winner, troops stay put.

text.p: Levon Ter-Petrosyan on Sunday was officially declared the winner of last week's controversial presidential election in Armenia, giving him five more years in office.
The Central Electoral Commission said Ter-Petrosyan received nearly 52 percent of the vote compared to less than 42 percent for his main opponent Vazgen Manukyan, a former prime minister.
Communist Sergei Badalyan got slightly over six percent. The turnout in the ballot last Sunday was 61 percent of the 2.21 million electorate.
Ter-Petrosyan received 19,715 votes -- less than two percent -- more than the 50 percent needed to avoid a second-round showdown with Manukyan.

The margin, even smaller than preliminary figures, is likely to add fire to allegations by Manukyan's camp that fraud and irregularities, also noted by international observers, influenced the result in Ter-Petrosyan's favor.
Observers say most of the abuses were committed by the president's supporters and electoral officials loyal to him. But they stopped short of declaring thje poll unfair.
Ter-Petrosyan aide Jerair Lipartyan said his boss would have no comment on the results until Monday, when he will address the nation on television.

Manukyan wasn't available to comment as he has gone into hiding, accused by Ter-Petrosyan of inspiring a rowdy protest last week in which some of his supporters broke into the country's parliament building and beat up the speaker and his deputy. The president said the melee was an attempted "fascist" coup by "mentally ill people."

Manukyan's whereabouts are unknown and his immunity from arrest as a presidential candidate has run out. Parliament, dominated by members of Ter-Petrosyan's ruling party, voted last week to press criminal charges over the rally against him and other opposition deputies.
Armenia's prosecutor said on Saturday four opposition members of parliament had been arrested.

Opposition figures say Ter-Petrosyan has used the unrest as a pretext to cover up what they say is his rigging of the results of the election and to wipe out dissent in the rocky country of 3.5 million tucked between Azerbaijan, Georgia, Iran, and Turkey.

Manukyan closed in on the president quickly in the closing days of campaigning, promising to raise living standards in the still impoverished country reeling from a long territorial conflict with Azerbaijan and the break-up of the Soviet Union.
Ter-Petrosyan, a 51-year old academic whom detractors accuse of having lost touch with reality, sent the army into the streets of Yerevan after the violence.
Most of the soldiers have now left but several hundreds of them, backed by light tanks, remain in key locations near the centre of the city of about one million.
Defense Minister Vazgen Sarkisyan, who has been directing his troops since they were deployed, has said publicly that the army would not let Manukyan take power in any case.
"After these events, even if he (Manukyan) got 100 percent of the vote, neither the army nor the interior ministry nor the security organs would accept him," he said last week.
Diplomats say as many as 200 political opponents of Ter- Petrosyan have been arrested over the last few days.
General prosecutor Artavazd Gevorkyan denied a large scale arrest campaign. "Rumors that allegedly there are mass arrests taking place are untrue," he said on Saturday.
